LqSdKtxPGNM.title: The Implications of Knowing: Finding Meaning
LqSdKtxPGNM.one_line: The second implication of knowing Allah: a meaningful life, stewardship as service, and why boredom and emptiness have no place for a Muslim.
LqSdKtxPGNM.summary: Continuing his series on what knowing Allah actually does for a person, the sheikh recalls the first implication, moral integrity, and moves to the second: meaning. Allah rejects the idea that He created people without purpose or accountability, created jinn and humans to know and serve Him, and gave them freedom and diversity so they would come to know one another. The oldest human fear is floating meaninglessly in an expanding void; knowing Allah, al-Haqq, the giver of meaning, removes that question. Meaning produces purpose, purpose drive, drive action; without it an inner void grows no matter what money, travel or pleasure is thrown at it, while even atheists who find a cause gain some fulfilment. So how can a Muslim be bored? Boredom is a modern word that does not fit a life with purpose. From Adam's appointment as khalifah he defines stewardship as caregiving on another's behalf, the way to serve a Lord who needs nothing: every role, parent, worker, student, is a service with meaning. The ummah has endless fronts needing work, locally and globally. In the second khutbah he warns against making the things created for us our purpose, and asks what two billion Muslims living purposefully would change, lamenting idle youth.

outline.heading: Destined for greatness

outline.gist: Local youth work, advocacy for Palestine and Sudan; some who do not know God live more meaningful lives than many Muslims.

outline.gist: Food, rivers, sun and stars were created for us; living to eat turns the order upside down.

outline.gist: Finding meaning is straightforward once one knows Allah is the Truth.

EYFoX7fvjrE.title: Tazkiyah Halaqah: Self-Value #42
EYFoX7fvjrE.one_line: From vanity to arrogance: confidence versus credit-taking, the ranking mind, racism, humility as reality, and Iblis's refusal to prostrate.
EYFoX7fvjrE.summary: He finishes his treatment of vanity and opens arrogance within the self-value module, arguing that the four diseases of the heart all stem from how we value ourselves. Vanity is claiming credit for outcomes when no one can know how much of a result is their own effort; that measure belongs to Allah on Judgment Day. Its opposite is confidence in the potential Allah created in you, not low self-esteem. Knowing you are skilled, if properly certified, is not vanity; attaching your worth to it is. Self-value anchored in Allah cannot be shaken the way worth tied to nation or family name can. Arrogance differs from vanity by involving others: the nafs, wired for survival, treats every newcomer as a threat, sizes them up and hunts for a flaw. Freed from deriving worth, a more advanced person becomes a resource. Racism is arrogance extended to a whole people, illustrated by the neighbouring village he was raised to despise. Humility is simply acknowledging reality: we are weak, made of earth, and equal. He closes with Iblis, a pious jinn raised among the angels who could not bring himself to honour Adam, and warns that thinking you would have obeyed in his place repeats his mistake.

outline.heading: Self-value as the root of ethics and the diseases of the heart
outline.gist: Self-value shapes the ethics we adopt; vanity, arrogance, showing off and envy all fall under this module.

outline.heading: Recap: the two-storey pendulum
outline.gist: When self-value swings, vanity and arrogance appear together; he has never seen a credible case of one without the other.

outline.heading: The opposite of vanity is confidence
outline.gist: Low self-esteem is vanity's mirror; the real opposite is confidence in the potential Allah created in you.

outline.heading: Vanity: claiming credit we cannot measure
outline.gist: No one, even materialistically, knows what share of an outcome is their effort; deciding that share takes over Allah's role.

outline.heading: Superficial humbleness feeds vanity
outline.gist: Acting humble to be seen as moral is one of the ugliest forms of self-manipulation.

outline.heading: Praise belongs to Allah
outline.gist: The Quran's first words settle who is praiseworthy; we are only praiseworthy if He declares it.

outline.heading: Knowing you are good at something is not vanity
outline.gist: Using medicine as an example: a physician can say he knows his field, but the cure is from Allah.

outline.heading: Competence needs certification
outline.gist: Islamic learning, like medicine, depends on being certified by qualified teachers, not self-appointed.

outline.heading: Anchoring self-value in the true constant
outline.gist: A secure self-value lets you take feedback; worth tied to country or family name can collapse, as displaced Palestinians and Iraqis found.

outline.heading: Good assumptions about others' efforts
outline.gist: Praise and credit others generously while withholding credit from yourself; this is the healthy Muslim mentality.

outline.heading: How arrogance differs from vanity
outline.gist: Vanity is between you and yourself; arrogance needs someone to compare against, as the thought experiment of a lone islander shows.

outline.heading: Neither praising nor hating yourself
outline.gist: Self-loathing over failure is common in Canada; review successes and failures objectively instead.

outline.heading: Arrogance is born from comparison
outline.gist: A variable self-value forces a constant, exhausting ranking of yourself against others.

outline.heading: The newcomer as a threat: the nafs' survival logic
outline.gist: The nafs sees every new person as competition for food, status and survival.

outline.heading: Sizing people up and hunting for one flaw
outline.gist: We fill gaps with assumptions, label strangers arrogant, and inflate a single flaw to feel better, as in the gym example.

outline.heading: From threat to resource
outline.gist: If you stop deriving worth from achievements, a more advanced person becomes a mentor rather than a rival.

outline.heading: An atom of arrogance bars Paradise
outline.gist: The hadith in Muslim shows arrogance reflects a systemic misunderstanding of one's value that cannot coexist with Paradise.

outline.heading: Racism at the root of conflict
outline.gist: Most wars and oppression, from Palestine to Syria to Africa, carry a core of one group seeing another as lesser.

outline.heading: The neighbouring village
outline.gist: He was raised to believe the next village were savages until high school showed him they were, if anything, better.

outline.heading: Racism as arrogance toward a whole people
outline.gist: Everyone holds some group they generalize about; such generalizations are almost always wrong, and Allah gave every human equal value.

outline.heading: The Prophet was humble at his core
outline.gist: He will show over coming sessions that humility defined the Prophet's character.

outline.heading: Saying 'I am humble' is arrogance
outline.gist: Claiming humility implies you came down from a higher place.

outline.heading: Humility is acknowledging reality
outline.gist: We are made of earth, weak and dependent, and equal except in taqwa; greatness belongs to Allah by nature, so humility in us is simply truth.

outline.heading: Clarifying humility versus lowering yourself
outline.gist: In answer to a question, he repeats that humility is not bringing yourself down but recognizing everyone's equal value.

outline.heading: Two Quranic stories of arrogance
outline.gist: Stories of Adam and Iblis are origin stories whose figurative lessons describe the permanent human struggle.

outline.heading: Iblis: a pious jinn raised among the angels
outline.gist: Jinn, like humans, can disobey; Iblis chose obedience so consistently that he was admitted among the angels.

outline.heading: The angels question a new creation
outline.gist: Their experience of jinn bloodshed made them ask why another creature with free choice was needed.

outline.heading: Prostration before Adam did anything
outline.gist: Adam had only shown his potential for knowledge, yet the angels honoured him; this is the source of innate human value.

outline.heading: Iblis could not bring himself to bow
outline.gist: He argued from merit and from nature, fire against foul clay, without openly challenging God.

outline.heading: Would you have prostrated?
outline.gist: Insisting you would have obeyed in his place is the same arrogance; the lesson is to ask how to change yourself.

SWPXycnrpZY.title: Guarding the Eyes: The Second Glance Is a Choice
SWPXycnrpZY.one_line: Closing a series on sins of the limbs: lowering the gaze, and asking what our limbs will testify about us.
SWPXycnrpZY.summary: The speaker concludes a short series on how the limbs of the body (tongue, ears, hands, feet) can become means of sin, ending with the eyes. He cites the hadith in Sahih Muslim in which Jarir ibn Abdullah asked the Prophet about the sudden, unintended glance, and was told to turn his eyes away. In a world where images appear without warning at school, at work, outside and especially on phones, we cannot always control what the eyes meet, but we are responsible for where we direct them next: the first glance may be sudden, the second is always chosen. He then ties the series together: the limbs are blessings and a trust from Allah, not independent of us, and small things such as an overheard conversation, a glance or a step toward wrong will weigh heavily on the record on the Day of Judgment. He closes by asking the audience to imagine their eyes, ears, tongue, hands and feet testifying about them today, and makes dua that every limb be a witness for them rather than against them.

FWuytlROnws.one_line: He begins reading al-Tirmidhi's Shama'il and explains why forming a mental image of the Prophet helps build a relationship with him.
FWuytlROnws.summary: He introduces the books Muslims read in this month about the Prophet, the Shifa of Qadi Iyad and the Shama'il of al-Tirmidhi, and presents al-Tirmidhi as both a collector of hadith and a critic of narrators. The Shama'il has almost no introduction; al-Tirmidhi simply lays out the narrations, and a few are weak in chain though none carries a meaning foreign to what is authentic. His plan, as last year, is to take one or two narrations from each chapter. He then answers why the Prophet's appearance matters at all. Allah cannot and must not be pictured, which is why the relationship with Him takes the most work. Humans build relationships partly through what they can see: body language and appearance do a great deal, for better or worse. The Prophet is the human bridge, so learning how he looked, walked, spoke and ate lets Muslims fourteen centuries later form an image and grow attached. He reads Anas's opening narration: neither very tall nor short, neither stark white nor dark, hair neither tightly curled nor straight; sent at forty, ten years in Makkah and ten in Madinah, taken at around sixty with fewer than twenty white hairs. He notes the book opens with a narration that sketches both his appearance and the outline of his life.

He then narrates the hadith in which Ali takes Thuwayr's father to visit al-Hasan, finds Abu Musa al-Ash'ari already there, and asks whether he came as a casual visitor or to tend to a sick man. d2kqO46M1Dc.summary: He explains the long tradition of reciting al-Tirmidhi's Shama'il in Rabi' al-Awwal, the month of the Prophet's birth, hijrah and death, and how hadith books were classically transmitted: students recite to the sheikh, who corrects and explains, and he wants to give a taste of that blessing. The first narration is al-Bara' ibn 'Azib's: medium height leaning tall, broad shoulders, a full head of hair reaching the earlobes, and a garment with red in it. He dwells on the broad shoulders as both literal and figurative: a man described this way is someone you can lean on. Al-Bara' ends that he never saw anything more beautiful. He explains why he reads narrations rather than listing features: each companion closes with what he felt, and people are known by how those closest to them felt about them. 77R0YPZFQ8U.summary: Continuing his series on bad religiosity, he notes how many examples the Prophet gave of religiosity that loses its function when a priority is missed. He narrates the hadith of a man on a long journey, dishevelled and dusty, raising his hands to the sky and calling on his Lord, yet his food, drink and clothing are unlawful and he was nourished on the unlawful, so how could he be answered? He stresses that everything about this man suggests humility and closeness: he is poor, exhausted, travelling and pleading. One neglected priority, earning and eating lawfully, undoes all of it. He links this to the verse that the supplication of those who reject is lost, and calls the idea terrifying for those who understand it, because Allah never otherwise refuses someone who turns to Him; He always accepts the repentant. He asks the audience to be careful with the lawfulness of what they consume so that they do not ruin everything else they do.

0-PXs9MgvgY.one_line: The five rights of a Muslim as the basis for caring for the sick, and why Muslims should protect public health care.
0-PXs9MgvgY.summary: Closing his short series on caring for the ill, he stresses that the duty is wider than visiting: donating blood and organs, arranging transport and supporting those who are struggling. He takes the hadith of the five rights a Muslim has over another as the strongest basis for the topic. Returning the greeting of peace is more than words: it answers a declaration of peace that a Muslim may not refuse. The second right, usually rendered as visiting the sick, really means caring for them, much as he goes to his clinic to care for patients, not to visit them. He argues this is the foundation for free health care in a Muslim society, since care for the ill is their right over the community. At a communal level that means ensuring access to medicine and professionals. Canada has such a system, and Muslims must take a civic and political interest in protecting it from sliding into a two-tier model. From oncology he gives the example of treatment plans costing around a million dollars a year that patients receive here at no cost. The remaining rights each carry social and spiritual meaning. He ends by urging everyone to donate blood and register as organ donors.

jOrnJktjMxc.summary: The speaker reads and explains the hadith in Sahih Muslim in which Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr reports the words the Prophet used to declare after every prayer: there is no god but Allah alone, His is the dominion and the praise, there is no power except by Allah, His is the blessing, the favour and the beautiful praise, sincere in religion to Him even if the disbelievers dislike it. Continuing a series from previous weeks, he notes that the dhikr begins and ends with la ilaha illa Allah, so everything returns to tawhid: wealth, power and career are only means, and nothing should occupy the heart except Allah. He goes through the phrases, tying 'His is the blessing' to sight, hearing, food, the ability to pray and fast, loved ones, security and a roof overhead. Repeating this after each prayer is how a forgetful, hasty and argumentative human being stays connected to Allah throughout the day.

0b8vatnEyGQ.one_line: A personal reminder on how community anchors faith, using the hadith of the wolf and the stray sheep and the HALT check.
0b8vatnEyGQ.summary: The speaker narrates the hadith that wherever three people do not establish congregational prayer, Shaytan overcomes them, so hold to the congregation, since the wolf only takes the stray sheep. He explains the image: the wolf attacks the sheep that wanders from the centre of the flock. He then shares his own experience of living alone for the first time, away from the masjid for about a year and a half, and how much harder it was to keep his relationship with Allah without people around him. Familiar faces in the masjid remind you of your faith without saying anything, and simply being present keeps you accountable. He closes with the HALT check from behavioural psychology: before acting or deciding, ask whether you are hungry, angry, lonely or tired, since these states make you vulnerable to choices you regret.

CvSMyyFYgvc.title: Awaken the Coach Within You
CvSMyyFYgvc.one_line: A guest talk on coaching: solution-focused questions, the brain and neuroplasticity, and the Prophet as a model coach.
CvSMyyFYgvc.summary: Prof. Louei Ali, a professional coach, gives an interactive community talk on coaching oneself and others. He opens with an exercise asking listeners to picture a challenge, the outcome they want and what they have not considered, then points out that he gave no advice. He tells how a client once told him he was a poor salesman but should be a coach. He contrasts command-and-control leadership, counselling and mentoring with coaching, which is solution-focused and rests on principles: people are whole, have the resources within them, and make the best choice available to them. Drawing on the reptilian, emotional and creative layers of the brain, studies of London taxi drivers and visualizing basketball free throws, he argues that safety and visualization unlock creative thinking. He covers rapport, listening for repeated words, powerful questions such as 'what else?', and accountability. He then presents the Prophet as the best coach: asking questions and waiting (the bankrupt, the tree like the believer, the river and the five prayers), gradual teaching, visual aids such as the lines drawn in the sand, one focused piece of advice ('do not get angry'), and patient rapport with the young man who asked permission for zina. He ends with homework: give less advice and ask more questions.

hU-dC_ubLR4.one_line: Feed the hungry, visit the sick, free the captive: the Prophet's three commands as a foundation for serving a community's weakest.
hU-dC_ubLR4.summary: The sheikh opens a few nights of reminders on caring for the ill, singling out the chronically ill as a forgotten group in every community. Care is broad: personal visits, blood donation, and organ donation, which major fatwa bodies have encouraged for two decades. He recalls a historical waqf, begun in Egypt and carried to Damascus, that paid people to stand outside a patient's room and speak of how well he was doing so he would overhear and take heart. He then presents the hadith of Abu Musa in which the Prophet, unusually, gave three consecutive commands: feed the hungry, visit the sick, and free the captive. True hunger, which most of the audience has never known even in long Ramadan fasts, devastates a person because there is no promise of food to come. Visiting means care, offering whatever the patient needs. Freeing the captive covers the imprisoned, the enslaved and the indebted. He reads this as the Prophet's social philosophy: look to the weakest, those lacking food, health ('afiyah) and freedom, and serve them first, because a community sails or sinks together. He frames this as an ethical conviction that, if Muslims lived it, would bring sustainable change.

1ADMhwDd92U.title: The Implications of Knowing God: Equanimity and Resilience
1ADMhwDd92U.one_line: The third implication of knowing God: since He knows and decrees everything, every ease and hardship has a clear response.
1ADMhwDd92U.summary: Continuing his series on what follows the moment a person knows there is a God, before any further learning, he recaps moral integrity and meaning, then gives the third implication: equanimity and resilience. If Allah is all-knowing and all-powerful, the future is within His knowledge and decree. Without Him, life is only worth living when you get what you want. He rejects the idea that ease proves Allah's love and hardship His contempt, drawing on Surah al-Fajr, and tells the occasion of Surah ad-Duha: after a pause in revelation the Prophet was taunted that his Lord had abandoned him, and Allah answered that He had not, that the hereafter is better, and reminded him how He sheltered, guided and enriched him. He cites hadith that even a thorn's prick expiates sins and that the believer's affair is all good. He then gives a framework of four cases: a logical good outcome calls for gratitude; a logical hardship calls for repentance and patience; an undeserved good calls for praise and repentance, because Allah bailed you out; an undeserved hardship calls for patience. A believer who truly knows Allah sees himself only in the middle two. Nothing arrives labelled good or evil: how we respond decides what it becomes. He urges people to study their deen properly rather than through short clips.

yOZXWIK3g4A.title: Bad Religiosity #12: The Bankrupt One
yOZXWIK3g4A.one_line: Closing the series with the hadith of the bankrupt one: worship cannot cancel out harm done to people.
yOZXWIK3g4A.summary: He closes his series on bad religiosity, religion that keeps its outward form but loses its essence because priorities are confused, with the best-known example the Prophet gave. He walks through the hadith of the bankrupt one: a man arrives on the Day of Judgment with prayer, fasting and zakat, but he cursed one person, harmed another, took wealth and violated honour. His wronged victims take from his good deeds, the only currency left, and when those run out their sins are put on him and he is thrown into the Fire. He insists the point is that worship and harm do not balance out; people's rights are a red line, and non-maleficence comes before rituals. He names the common pattern of someone vicious at work who feels safe because he sits in the first row at the masjid. He cites a related narration of a man whose deeds rise before him until he thinks he is saved, then lose them. To him this is less about tyranny than ordinary carelessness with temper and with how one treats people judged unworthy. He asks everyone to learn where the absolute lines are.

outline.gist: Rights owed to people must be settled before Paradise, and the only currency is good deeds.

5-MXc4EMH54.title: Tazkiyah Halaqah: Self-Value #43 – Arrogance, Assumptions and the Fall of Iblis
5-MXc4EMH54.one_line: Arrogance grows from bad assumptions that dehumanize others; understanding people without agreeing or accepting, illustrated through Iblis, Abu Jahl and a personal exercise.
5-MXc4EMH54.summary: The sheikh continues the module on self-value with its second layer of arrogance: how we see other people. Since Allah created everyone equal and anyone can rise or fall by their choices at any moment, there is nothing to prove; chasing worth by comparison is like a drug, and giving it up feels dull at first. People prefer painful truth to a comfortable lie, and only a truthful view of oneself allows real connection with Allah. Arrogance toward others runs on assumptions: we fill the gaps in their stories with bad guesses so the ego can rank them below us. The ideal is no assumptions, otherwise good ones, except where one is a caregiver or protector. Arrogance dehumanizes, and racism is collective arrogance that makes mass killing thinkable. He returns to Iblis, who filled gaps about Adam and let arrogance block a direct command, and warns that saying 'I would have obeyed' repeats the same trap. He separates understanding from agreeing and accepting, applying it to Abu Jahl, to non-Muslims, and to the LGBTQ movement, which must be understood in order to guard against it. He invites listeners to serve someone they dislike, recounting how this changed him at eighteen.

outline.heading: Self-value and the swinging pendulum
outline.gist: Most diseases of the heart stem from misreading self-value, swinging between vanity and low self-esteem until late in life.

outline.heading: Created equal, with potential at every moment
outline.gist: Everyone is created equal and can head to the highest or lowest ranks at any moment, so there is nothing to prove; human value is divine and untouched by applause or hatred.

outline.heading: Motivation without proving yourself: pampering and pressure
outline.gist: Pampered children lose drive, while parents who make children prove themselves can leave a lasting sense of never being worthy.

outline.heading: The motives Allah provides
outline.gist: Paradise, His love and pleasure, and the identities of khalifah and servant are meant to drive good deeds instead of comparison.

outline.heading: Comparison as a drug: the dullness of coming off it
outline.gist: Like an addict getting clean, a person who stops feeding on superiority feels flat at first before real joy returns.

outline.heading: Each of us can choose our rank right now
outline.gist: At this very moment any person can make a choice that sends them to the highest or lowest ranks, and that is what matters.

outline.heading: Nobody wants to live a lie: the betrayed spouse
outline.gist: Discovering years of infidelity hurts most because the happiness was unreal.

outline.heading: Hiding a cancer diagnosis
outline.gist: From his oncology practice: families in the East hide fatal diagnoses, but patients are always upset when they learn they lived a lie.

outline.heading: Why the plain truth of the Quran feels flat
outline.gist: We rely on beautiful voices to feel the Quran because our emotions are built on false self-images; clarity about self-value brings khushu.

outline.heading: Truthfulness with oneself as a condition for connecting with Allah
outline.gist: Without honesty in how we see ourselves and others we cannot connect with Allah; feeling better when others fail means feeling worse when they succeed.

outline.heading: Arrogance toward others runs on assumptions
outline.gist: We never know anyone's full story, so we fill the gaps, and we fill them with bad things when we feel threatened.

outline.heading: No assumptions, or else good ones
outline.gist: The right answer is to assume nothing because we should be too busy; if we must assume, assume good.

outline.heading: When bad assumptions are obligatory
outline.gist: Caregivers and protectors, such as parents, business guardians and a father screening a suitor, must assume the worst.

outline.heading: The ego's ranking system
outline.gist: The nafs compares looks, wealth and education, then digs for character or religious flaws so it can place others below itself.

outline.heading: Arrogance dehumanizes: racism as collective arrogance
outline.gist: Denying people their story is dehumanization; racism does this to whole groups and makes mass killing justifiable, as on this land.

outline.heading: If it was a choice, I could make it too
outline.gist: Because all humans are equal, evil is a choice, which means we carry the same potential; that is why the Quran repeats these stories.

outline.heading: Iblis's logic before the command to prostrate
outline.gist: The angels asked and obeyed; Iblis reasoned from his merit and his fiery origin against Adam's clay, while still knowing Allah well.

outline.heading: Would you have obeyed? The trap of certainty
outline.gist: Claiming we would have obeyed is itself the arrogance of Iblis; all we can have is hope and dua.

outline.heading: Good assumptions in the slander of Aisha
outline.gist: The Quran says believers should have thought well of themselves; Abu Ayyub and his wife reasoned that if they would not do it, Aisha and Safwan would not either.

outline.heading: Understanding versus agreeing versus accepting
outline.gist: Understanding how a wrong could happen is not agreeing it was right in the situation nor accepting it as no sin; it is how we protect ourselves.

outline.heading: How Iblis filled the gaps about Adam
outline.gist: Iblis credited himself for his status, then had to think badly of Adam, the new steward, to justify not feeling lesser.

outline.heading: Arrogance can block a direct command of Allah
outline.gist: The moral: arrogance can grow until it stands between a person and obeying Allah directly.

outline.heading: Abu Jahl and the rivalry with Banu Hashim
outline.gist: Raised to see his clan as better, Abu Jahl admitted the Prophet was truthful yet refused to follow a man of Banu Hashim.

outline.heading: The same arrogance, untested, in us
outline.gist: We are no different from Abu Jahl; our arrogance simply has not been exposed by a test.

outline.heading: The exercise: serve someone you dislike
outline.gist: His own teacher made him serve a man who had made his life hard; after refusing twice he did it, and the man became a close friend.

outline.heading: What changed: humanizing the other person
outline.gist: Picturing the man's life and his own faults removed the dehumanizing label; he understood without agreeing or accepting.

outline.heading: An honest invitation to try it
outline.gist: Choose someone genuinely disliked, not an oppressor, and serve them; the exercise teaches more about yourself than all his lectures.

outline.heading: Understanding people of other faiths
outline.gist: As a minority among many faiths, Muslims must understand others or they will dehumanize them; all humanity is the Prophet's ummah of invitation.

outline.heading: Understanding the LGBTQ movement in order to guard against it
outline.gist: Not agreeing or accepting, but understanding where it comes from, because those who refuse to understand have no tools to deal with it.

outline.heading: Building the ability to understand without agreeing
outline.gist: Tackling arrogance requires firmly separating these concepts.

outline.heading: What stopped you? I am better than him
outline.gist: Allah's question hints that something inside stopped Iblis; his answer was pure self-value.

outline.heading: Iblis did not dare cite his piety
outline.gist: Even Iblis did not use his worship as grounds for superiority, which makes religious arrogance among Muslims baffling.

outline.heading: The despised clay was Adam's strength
outline.gist: Arrogance misjudges exactly what is valuable: Adam's mix of clay, water and spirit, like rotting soil that brings forth life, is what made him unique.

outline.heading: Arrogant, or superior by nature?
outline.gist: Allah asks whether Iblis became arrogant or is of the exalted; only Allah is al-Ali, and no creature is superior by nature.

outline.heading: Respite and the vow to misguide
outline.gist: Iblis asks for time to prove humans unworthy and to lead them by the reins into Hell.

outline.heading: Allah's reply and Iblis's first trick
outline.gist: Allah grants the request but denies him power over His true servants; Iblis's main trick is to make us arrogant as he became.

1QIqy5MQ4yI.title: Bounties of Taking Care of the Sick #3
1QIqy5MQ4yI.one_line: Two hadith in Musnad Ahmad: whoever cares for the sick is in the harvest of Paradise and is promised a place in it.
1QIqy5MQ4yI.summary: Continuing his short nightly series on caring for the ill and especially the chronically ill, the sheikh combines two short, similar hadith from the Musnad of Imam Ahmad with authentic chains. He first reminds the audience that care takes many forms beyond a visit, pointing again to blood donation, which hospitals are always short of, and to organ donation after death. The first narration says that whoever visits or cares for a sick person remains in the khurfah of Paradise. He explains the word: not a room, but the harvest, the fruit-bearing part, from the Arabic logic of working through the season and then gathering the yield. The second says a caller from the heavens declares that the visitor has done well, his steps are blessed, and he has taken up a dwelling in Paradise. So caring for the ill puts a person in Paradise while doing it and secures a place there later, with Allah's pleasure throughout. He ends by turning the series inward: it is also a reminder to be grateful for health, and for those already ill, to be grateful for whatever health remains, because that too can be lost.

outline.heading: Two short hadith and the many forms of care
outline.gist: Introduces two narrations from Musnad Ahmad and repeats that care goes beyond visiting.

outline.heading: Blood and organ donation as service to the ill
outline.gist: Hospitals are often short of blood units; donating blood and organs serves the sick.

outline.heading: In the harvest of Paradise: the meaning of khurfah
outline.gist: The carer remains in the fruit-bearing part of Paradise; he explains the Arabic sense of harvesting after a season of work.

outline.heading: A caller from heaven: your steps are blessed
outline.gist: The second narration: a caller declares the visitor has done well and has secured a dwelling in Paradise.

outline.heading: Gratitude for the health we still have
outline.gist: The series is also a call to thank Allah for health, and for the sick to value what health remains.
